Heart Murmurs in an Adult

shape first, then breathing · the click and the second heart sound (S2) decide · prior congenital repair can explain adult complications

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Identify systolic, diastolic or continuous timing, then use site, radiation, breathing, the click and second heart sound (S2) to choose the lesion.
  • Inspiration usually accentuates right-sided murmurs. Standing or Valsalva accentuates hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and shifts a prolapse click earlier.
  • In a patient with repaired tetralogy of Fallot, think pulmonic regurgitation; palpitations with syncope require evaluation for ventricular arrhythmia.

Right inspiration, left expiration (RILE): breathing helps localize the murmur. A repaired congenital lesion can explain the adult presentation.

2Urgent risks
High-risk presentations
FindingAction
Syncope, angina or exertional dyspnea with an aortic ejection murmurArrange prompt echocardiography and valve assessment.
Palpitations or syncope after tetralogy repairObtain an electrocardiogram (ECG), ambulatory rhythm monitoring and specialist assessment.
Exertional syncope with a dynamic systolic murmur and a sudden-death family historyEvaluate urgently for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; ventricular arrhythmia can cause sudden death in young athletes.
3Differential
Murmur patterns
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Pulmonic (pulmonary) stenosisEjection click and crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left upper sternal border; wide S2 split varies with breathing.Confirm the valve obstruction and gradient with Doppler echo.
Atrial septal defectWide, fixed S2 split; increased pulmonic flow without a stenotic-valve click.Obtain echocardiography to define the shunt.
Tricuspid regurgitationHolosystolic murmur at the lower left sternal border, louder on inspiration; moderate to severe disease may cause prominent venous waves, and severe disease may cause a pulsatile liver.Use echo to assess the regurgitation and right ventricular (RV) size; identify the cause.
Mitral regurgitationHolosystolic apical murmur with axillary radiation.Obtain echo to assess the valve and ventricle.
Aortic stenosisCrescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids; softer with Valsalva. A bicuspid valve can present prematurely.Confirm with transthoracic echo.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathySystolic ejection murmur becomes louder with standing or Valsalva, softer with squatting or handgrip.Obtain echo to assess dynamic outflow obstruction.
Aortic regurgitationEarly diastolic decrescendo murmur with a wide pulse pressure.Obtain echo to quantify regurgitation.
Pulmonic (pulmonary) regurgitationEarly diastolic murmur after repaired tetralogy; with pulmonary hypertension, a loud pulmonic component of S2 (P2) suggests a Graham Steell murmur.Order echocardiography to assess regurgitation and RV dilation.
Mitral or tricuspid stenosisDiastolic rumble; an apical opening snap favors mitral stenosis, inspiration favors the tricuspid valve.Use echo to define the obstructed valve.
Mitral valve prolapseA mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur; standing moves the click earlier.Order echocardiography if structural disease or associated regurgitation is suspected.
Functional flow murmurSoft systolic murmur, no click, normal S2 and a high-output cause such as anemia or fever.Treat the underlying cause; reassess the murmur.
Left atrial myxomaA diastolic plop or position-dependent rumble with constitutional symptoms; myxoma is the most common primary cardiac tumor in adults.Obtain echo to look for a mass.
Patent ductus arteriosusA continuous, machine-like murmur spans S2.Obtain echo to define the shunt.
Heart sounds: first (S1) and second (S2)
S2 findingInterpretation
Wide split that varies with respirationDelayed pulmonic closure, as in pulmonic stenosis.
Wide, fixed splitAtrial septal defect.
Paradoxical splittingDelayed aortic closure, as in severe aortic stenosis or left bundle branch block.
Loud P2Pulmonary hypertension; with a pulmonary diastolic murmur, consider Graham Steell.
Single S2Several congenital or severe valve conditions can merge or remove a component; use the complete examination.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Prior tetralogy repair and a new diastolic murmurPulmonic regurgitationOrder echo to assess RV size and regurgitation; obtain rhythm monitoring for palpitations or syncope.
A wide fixed split rather than a variable splitAtrial septal defect rather than isolated pulmonic stenosisConfirm the shunt with echo.
Pause point
Early diastolic or holosystolic murmur Named by its shape alone Match both the phase and the side → Aortic and pulmonic regurgitation share an early diastolic shape; tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic
Treatment by cause
CauseAction
Severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosisRefer for balloon valvuloplasty when the valve anatomy is suitable.
Pulmonic regurgitation after repairFollow RV size and function; symptoms with progressive dilation or impaired function can require pulmonary valve replacement.
Tricuspid regurgitation or Graham Steell murmurIdentify and treat the cause of tricuspid regurgitation, including intrinsic valve disease. A Graham Steell murmur requires treatment of the pulmonary hypertension.
After congenital heart repairThe repair can determine the adult complication
Tetralogy of FallotPulmonic regurgitation, RV dilation and ventricular arrhythmia risk.Palpitations or syncope need rhythm evaluation.
Aortic valvotomyAortic regurgitation.
Coarctation repairRecurrent narrowing or persistent hypertension.
FontanProtein-losing enteropathy and arrhythmia.
Mustard or SenningBaffle obstruction or systemic RV failure.
Practice
  1. 30-year-old man has exertional dyspnea tetralogy of Fallot repaired at age 3 decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border, louder with inspiration single S2; parasternal heave Afebrile · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 84/min → Pulmonic regurgitation → The repaired tetralogy and right-sided diastolic murmur favor pulmonic regurgitation. Echocardiography assesses regurgitation and RV size; progressive symptomatic RV dilation warrants valve replacement assessment.
  2. 18-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur ejection click, then a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace widely split S2 that varies with respiration Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Pulmonic valve stenosis → an ejection click and a widened split that varies with breathing are pulmonic stenosis; an atrial septal defect splits S2 wide but fixed, with no click, and the innocent pulmonic flow murmur has no click and a normal S2; confirm with echocardiography
  3. 38-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap loud S1 ECG shows atrial fibrillation Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 112/min, irregularly irregular → Mitral stenosis → An apical diastolic rumble with an opening snap favors mitral stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis is accentuated by inspiration; a positional plop or rumble suggests a myxoma.
  4. 17-year-old boy is evaluated for a murmur harsh crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left mid-sternal border louder with Valsalva and on standing Family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 120/74 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy → Standing and Valsalva reduce filling and accentuate the dynamic outflow murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valve usually radiates toward the carotids; pulmonic stenosis is left upper sternal and accentuated by inspiration. Confirm the obstruction with echocardiography.
  5. 64-year-old man has leg edema and ascites distended jugular veins with large v waves pulsatile, tender, enlarged liver holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration Afebrile · BP 116/72 mm Hg · HR 88/min → Tricuspid regurgitation → A holosystolic murmur accentuated by inspiration, with venous v waves and hepatic pulsation, favors tricuspid regurgitation. Mitral regurgitation usually radiates toward the axilla; a ventricular septal defect is usually a harsh lower sternal murmur.
  6. 45-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur that decreases with inspiration bounding pulses No history of heart surgery or lung disease Afebrile · BP 158/52 mm Hg, a wide pulse pressure · HR 76/min → Aortic regurgitation → An early diastolic murmur with bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure favors aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic regurgitation is right-sided; mitral stenosis causes an apical rumble.
  7. 20-year-old woman has 6 months of heavy menstrual periods soft midsystolic murmur normal S2; no click No syncope or chest pain on exertion Afebrile · BP 110/68 mm Hg · HR 96/min · hemoglobin 8 g/dL → Functional flow murmur → Anemia can cause a soft systolic flow murmur. A normal S2 and absent click support that pattern here; Pulmonic valve stenosis usually has an ejection click and a variable split; an atrial septal defect has a fixed split. Treat the anemia and reassess the murmur.
  8. 55-year-old woman has dyspnea that changes with body position a plop and a rumble that vary with body position fever and weight loss T 38.1 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 92/min → Left atrial myxoma → a plop and a rumble that shift with position, with fever and weight loss, are a left atrial myxoma; mitral stenosis gives an apical rumble with an opening snap, and fever with weight loss also fit endocarditis, but a plop and rumble that shift with position point to a mass
  9. 20-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur midsystolic murmur at the left upper sternal border S2 split widely, and fixed with breathing; no click Lungs clear; no edema Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Atrial septal defect → a wide, fixed split with no click is an atrial septal defect, more right-sided flow across a normal pulmonic valve; pulmonic stenosis splits S2 widely but the split varies, after an ejection click, and tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic at the lower border
  10. 78-year-old man is evaluated after an episode of syncope crescendo-decrescendo murmur radiating to the carotids softer with Valsalva delayed carotid upstroke No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 128/84 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Aortic stenosis → Carotid radiation, a delayed upstroke and reduced intensity with Valsalva favor aortic stenosis. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy becomes louder as preload falls; mitral regurgitation is holosystolic.
  11. 28-year-old man has 2 weeks of palpitations and one episode of syncope repaired tetralogy of Fallot No chest pain, fever or seizure activity Afebrile · BP 116/70 mm Hg · HR 92/min → Ventricular arrhythmia → Palpitations with syncope after tetralogy repair require ECG, ambulatory monitoring and specialist assessment for ventricular arrhythmia. Pulmonic regurgitation with RV dilation can be the substrate.
  12. 30-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur decrescendo diastolic murmur at the left upper sternal border loud P2 echocardiogram shows pulmonary hypertension No prior heart surgery Afebrile · BP 118/76 mm Hg · HR 80/min → Graham Steell murmur → Graham Steell is pulmonic regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension: a loud P2 in pulmonary hypertension, contrasted with the prior congenital-repair setting, and there was no surgery; aortic regurgitation brings a wide pulse pressure, and this one is normal; treat the pulmonary hypertension
  13. 28-year-old woman is evaluated for a murmur mid-systolic click followed by a late systolic murmur the click moves earlier on standing No family history of sudden death Afebrile · BP 108/68 mm Hg · HR 72/min → Mitral valve prolapse → a click that moves earlier with standing (reduced preload) is mitral valve prolapse; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy also grows louder with reduced preload but is a harsh diamond-shaped murmur, and aortic stenosis has no mid-systolic click and gets softer with reduced preload
  14. 22-year-old woman has exertional dyspnea ejection click and a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the left 2nd interspace echocardiogram shows a doming pulmonic valve with a severe gradient Afebrile · BP 112/70 mm Hg · HR 84/min → Percutaneous balloon valvulotomy → congenital pulmonic stenosis, often silent until adult exertional dyspnea, now severe and symptomatic: percutaneous balloon valvulotomy is preferred over surgical replacement, and a severe, symptomatic valve is past observation
  15. 52-year-old man is evaluated for a murmur systolic murmur at the right 2nd interspace S2 splits paradoxically ECG shows no bundle branch block Afebrile · BP 134/82 mm Hg · HR 70/min → Aortic stenosis of a bicuspid valve → An aortic ejection murmur with paradoxical S2 splitting supports aortic stenosis. Premature adult presentation suggests a bicuspid valve; echocardiography establishes the lesion.
  16. 30-year-old man has worsening exertional dyspnea repaired tetralogy of Fallot echocardiogram shows a severely regurgitant pulmonic valve right ventricle more dilated than a year ago Afebrile · BP 118/72 mm Hg · HR 86/min → Pulmonic valve replacement → severe pulmonic regurgitation after repair with progressive right ventricular dilation and symptoms needs pulmonic valve replacement; serial echocardiography is surveillance, and diuretics with a recheck in a year leave the dilating ventricle untreated
Common wrong answers Tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic and grows with inspiration; a pulmonic ejection click and variable split instead favor stenosis. Aortic regurgitation is an early diastolic left-sided murmur, often with a wide pulse pressure. Atrial septal defect has a wide fixed split. A soft systolic murmur with anemia, no click and a normal S2 supports a flow murmur; reassess after treating the cause rather than using S2 alone to exclude valve disease.
Pairs with Heart Murmurs in a Child: the innocent pulmonic flow murmur, the benign counterpart of pulmonic stenosis; ask: is there a click, and what is S2 doing? Congenital Heart Disease: when a murmur appears and why; this brief covers what the murmur is.
Transferable rule

Fix phase and side before you name a valve, and check inspiration in every murmur. Then separate look-alikes by the accompanying findings, not the sound.
